title: Brewer's Conjecture and the CAP Theorem (2000-2002)
explainer: At a 2000 symposium, Eric Brewer proposed that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties at once - consistency, availability, and partition tolerance - and in 2002 Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch published a formal proof turning the conjecture into a theorem. The result forces an explicit design choice whenever a network can partition, which is why distributed databases describe themselves as roughly 'AP' or 'CP' systems rather than claiming to satisfy everything at once. It remains the most-cited reason distributed systems can't just be 'correct' the way a single-machine program can.

title: Lamport Clocks and Ordering Events Without a Shared Clock (1978)
explainer: In 1978, Leslie Lamport showed that processes without synchronized physical clocks can still agree on a consistent ordering of events, by having each process keep a counter that advances on every event and travels along with every message it sends. This 'happened-before' partial ordering underlies how distributed systems determine which of two concurrent updates came first and underlies the vector clocks and version-tracking schemes used in many modern distributed databases. The lesson's treatment of ordering and consistency across nodes traces directly back to this one paper.
